newsitem.title: USA: Ag sector crimp if ethanol break tax ends -- USDA.
newsitem.headline: Ag sector crimp if ethanol break tax ends -- USDA.

text.p: Ethanol production would fall sharply and net farm income drop by $1 billion a year if the U.S. Congress eliminated the ethanol tax break, an Agriculture Department report said Tuesday.

"We believe that elimination of the federal ethanol tax exemption would halt investment in ethanol production facilities...Ethanol production could decline by 50 to 100 percent from projections contained in the presidents FY1998 budget," acting Agriculture Undersecretary Catherine Woteki wrote in summarizing the report.
Farm income could drop $5.9-$10.2 billion in FY1998-2005.
Senator Tom Harkin, Iowa Democrat, released Woteki's summary of the report and it proved the value of the home-grown fuel.

"As we enter the budget (debate), there will be an opportunity to change the tax code," Harkin said. "I'm sending a clear message to the backers of big oil in Congress -- they're in for a fight if they go after ethanol."
The chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, Texas Republican Bill Archer, has said he wants to examine the exemption granted to ethanol from fuel taxes.
Last year, House Speaker Newt Gingrich sided with farm-state lawmakers to block an attack on the ethanol break.
Ethanol has been listed among possible "corporate welfare" items for reform this year.
Critics say the long-running tax break is an unjustified boon to distillers and an unfair advantage for the fuel.

The USDA report said elimination of the ethanol break would increase the trade deficit by as much as $7.8 billion during FY1998-2005 due to larger oil imports; reduce employment at ethanol plants by 2,050 to 4,100 workers and reduce cash receipts by farmers by $12-$20.8 billion in FY1998-2005.
